items.a: Yes. Groups, people, expenses, currencies, offline use and settling up are unlimited on the free tier. Plus exists for the features with a running cost behind them — receipt scanning, photo storage and extra devices. There is no card at sign-up and no trial that expires.

items.q: What is the difference between Plus and Pro?
items.a: Plus adds 300 receipt scans a month, use on up to 3 devices and bigger exports, imports and backups. Pro includes everything in Plus and adds the advanced AI voice agent with 150 commands a month. In India Plus is ₹49 a month (₹499 a year) and Pro is ₹99 a month (₹999 a year).

items.q: Does everyone need to install the app?
items.a: No. Share a link or a QR code and people can join and see the group in a browser, with no account and no download. They can create an account later if they want the app, and the ledger follows them.

items.q: What do you do with my data?
items.a: As little as we can. The ledger on your device is encrypted at rest, receipt photos can stay on your device or in your own cloud storage, and there is no advertising and no data selling. The shared ledger is on our server because that is what lets several phones agree — it is not end-to-end encrypted, and we would rather say so plainly.

items.q: Can I import or export my data?
items.a: Yes. Exporting your ledger is part of the free plan, and your data is yours to take with you. Plus raises the limits for bigger exports, imports and backups.

items.q: Can I add expenses by voice?
items.a: Yes. Everyone gets a voice allowance. Pro adds the advanced AI voice agent with 150 commands a month.

items.q: What happens when I have no signal?
items.a: Adding, editing and splitting keep working. Waves writes every expense to your phone first, so none of it needs the network. When you reconnect it syncs in the background and reconciles anything that changed while you were away.

items.q: Does Waves work with more than one currency?
items.a: Yes. Every amount is stored in the currency it was spent in, as whole minor units rather than as a decimal, so nothing drifts. You can fix the exchange rate you actually got for one bill, for one person, or for a whole trip, and every ISO 4217 currency is supported.

No, and that is deliberate. Waves works out who pays whom and how much, then hands that to a payment app you already use — a bank transfer, UPI, Pix, SEPA, PayNow, Venmo, PayPal or cash. Your money never passes through us, and Waves is not a bank.

Waves is not tied to a payment network or a banking licence, so there is nothing to roll out country by country — you can use it wherever you can install the app or open the web app. UPI settle-up is built for India, and other payment apps work the same way: Waves hands over the amount and you pay.

mcpPage.metaTitle: Connect an AI agent to Waves (MCP)
mcpPage.metaDescription: Connect Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any MCP client to your Waves ledger: the address, setup steps, every tool, what it can never do, and how to disconnect.
mcpPage.title: Connect your AI assistant to Waves
mcpPage.subtitle: Waves speaks MCP, the Model Context Protocol. Connect an assistant and it can read your groups and add expenses for you, as you, with the same rules the app follows. It is optional, and off until you set it up.
what: MCP is a standard way for an AI assistant to use software that is not itself. With Waves connected you can ask things like “what do I owe from the Goa trip” or “split last night’s dinner four ways”, and it reads and writes the same ledger the app does.

It connects to your account, not to Waves in general. An assistant you sign in sees what you see when you open the app: your groups, the people in them and the money between you. It cannot see a group you are not in, and nobody else’s assistant can see yours.
mcpPage.signinIntro: It is the ordinary OAuth flow, and your client does all of it. You only paste the address.
signin: Add the server in your client. It calls Waves and is told it needs to sign in.
A Waves page opens. You sign in and see which application is asking, then approve or refuse.
The assistant now acts as you. Refusing is a normal outcome and the application is told.
mcpPage.signinNote: Waves does not vouch for anybody else’s software, and the approval screen says so. Approve only assistants you chose to install.
mcpPage.setupIntro: Pick your client. If a menu is worded differently in your version, look for “add a custom connector” or “add an MCP server”.

tabs.name: Claude
steps: Open Claude on the web or the desktop app and go to the connectors settings.
Add a custom connector, paste the server address above, and save.
Press Connect. A Waves page opens in your browser: sign in and approve.
Start a chat and ask about your groups.
tabs.after: Then run /mcp inside Claude Code and choose Waves to sign in.

tabs.name: ChatGPT
steps: In ChatGPT, open the settings and look for connectors. If it asks, turn on developer mode. Custom connectors are not on every plan.
Add a new connector, name it Waves, and paste the server address above as the MCP server URL.
If it asks for authentication, choose OAuth.
Create it, then sign in and approve on the Waves page that opens.

tabs.name: Cursor
steps: Open the MCP settings, or edit mcp.json in your home .cursor folder (or .cursor/mcp.json inside a project).
Add the entry below and save.
Cursor shows Waves as needing sign-in. Choose it, approve in the browser, and the tools appear.

tabs.name: VS Code
steps: Create .vscode/mcp.json in your project, or run “MCP: Add Server” from the command palette and choose HTTP.
Add the entry below and save.
Start the server from the file. VS Code opens the Waves sign-in; approve it and the tools are available in chat.

tabs.name: Any MCP client
steps: Add a remote MCP server that uses streamable HTTP, with the address above.
Your client must support OAuth sign-in. It finds where to sign in on its own: an unauthenticated call is answered with 401 and a pointer to the metadata document below.
Most clients register themselves with the sign-in server, so there is nothing else to copy. If yours asks for a client ID, write to us.
Replies are plain JSON over POST. There is no session and no event stream.
tabs.snippetLabel: Check the address from a terminal
tabs.after: A 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header means the server is up and waiting for sign-in.

mcpPage.toolsIntro: These are all the tools Waves offers an assistant, and nothing else. Every write is a named, validated operation, not raw database access.
mcpPage.toolsNote: Amounts travel as whole minor units (paise or cents), never as floating point.

toolDoes.whoami: Says which account the assistant is acting as.
toolDoes.list_members: Lists the people in a group.
toolDoes.get_balances: Shows who owes what in a group, per person and currency.
toolDoes.settlement_plan: Shows who should pay whom to settle a group, plus payments waiting to be confirmed.
toolDoes.list_settlements: Lists the settlements recorded in a group and whether they are confirmed.
toolDoes.list_expenses: Lists a group’s expenses, newest first.
toolDoes.list_agent_writes: Lists everything an assistant has changed on your behalf.
toolDoes.payment_link: Builds a UPI or PayPal link for you to open and pay in your own app. Nothing is paid by building it.
toolDoes.create_group: Creates a group with you as its admin.
toolDoes.add_expense: Adds an expense to a group. The split is recomputed by Waves, not trusted from the assistant.
toolDoes.add_expense_with_person: Adds an expense between you and one person, in your one-to-one group with them.
toolDoes.edit_expense: Corrects an expense by adding a new version. History is kept.
toolDoes.delete_expense: Removes an expense. It is a soft delete and the group can see it.
toolDoes.record_settlement: Writes down that one member paid another. It does not pay anyone.
toolDoes.add_people: Adds people to a group by name, as members without an account yet.
toolDoes.invite_link: Returns the group’s join link to send to someone.

never: No tool pays anybody. Recording a settlement writes down that a payment happened. The paying stays something you do, in your own banking app, on purpose.
Every request runs under your own account with the same database rules as the app. There is no admin key in this path and no way to run raw queries.
A single expense and a single settlement each have a ceiling, and there is a further daily ceiling on what an assistant can write for you. The limits are enforced in the database.
It cannot hide what it did
Every change an assistant makes is recorded. Ask it “what did you change today?” and it reads that record back to you.
revoke: Remove Waves from your assistant’s connectors (or delete the entry from mcp.json). That deletes the credentials the assistant was holding, and it stops.
To cut an assistant off right now, write to us and say so. The app does not yet have a screen that lists the assistants connected through this address.
Check what one has done by asking it, or see the tools list_agent_writes above. Writes you made in the app yourself are not in that record.
self: There is also a local server for people working from the source repository. It runs on your own machine over stdio and signs in with a six-digit code sent to your email. It exists for development; use the hosted address above otherwise.
Set WAVES_MCP_READONLY=1 and only the reading tools are registered at all, so an assistant cannot attempt a write it was never offered.
faq: No. Nothing happens until you add the address to an assistant and approve it. Waves works the same whether or not you ever do.
Can an assistant pay my friends?
No. It can write down that you settled up and hand you a payment link, but you open the link and pay in your own app.
Will my group see what it adds?
Yes. An expense an assistant adds is a real entry in the group, like one you added yourself. Try it on a throwaway group first.
Not on the hosted address. Most assistants ask before running a tool that changes something, so keep that on. The local server has a read-only mode.
My client cannot connect. What now?
Check that the address is exactly as shown, ending in /api/mcp, and that your client supports OAuth sign-in for remote servers. If it still fails, write to us with the client name.
